text: Accelerating the sulfur redox kinetics in weakly-solvating lithium‒sulfur batteries under lean-electrolyte conditions Zi-Xian Chen a,b, Jia-Jia Zhao a,b, Guan-Ya Fang a,b, Shuo Zhang a,b, Jin Ma c,d, Meng Zhao c, Bo-Quan Li a,b,*, Jia-Qi Huang a,b,* a School of Materials Science and Engineering, Beijing Institute of Technology, Beijing 100081, China b Advanced Research Institute of Multidisciplinary Science, Beijing Institute of Technology, Beijing 100081, China c Beijing Key Laboratory of Complex Solid State Batteries & Tsinghua Center for Green Chemical Engineering Electrification, Department of Chemical Engineering, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China d Shanxi Research Institute for Clean Energy, Tsinghua University, Taiyuan 030032, China A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Lithium‒sulfur battery Lithium polysulfide Weakly-solvating electrolyte Lean electrolyte Sulfur redox kinetics A B S T R A C T Lithium–sulfur (Li–S) batteries are promising in realizing high energy density but hindered by limited cycling lifespan due to the corrosion of lithium metal anode by soluble lithium polysulfides.

Employing weakly-solvating electrolyte effectively prolongs the cycling lifespan via suppressing the anode corrosion but inevitably results in severe cathode capacity degradation under lean-electrolyte conditions.
Herein, the lean-electrolyte sulfur redox kinetics is systematically evaluated in weakly-solvating Li‒S batteries to guide target kinetic promotion strategy design.
High activation polarization caused by sluggish interfacial charge transfer kinetics is identified as the key limiting factor by polarization decoupling.
Smaller Li2S nuclei and thinner Li2S deposition are formed to render reduced deposition capacity.

To overcome the above challenge, a bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide lithium electrolyte is designed to realize a discharge capacity of 984 mAh g−1 at 0.2 C under a lean electrolyte volume of 5 μL mg−1 in weakly-solvating Li–S batteries.
This work affords rational guidance for accelerating the sulfur redox kinetics toward lean-electrolyte and weakly-solvating Li‒S batteries. 1.
Introduction The low-altitude economy constitutes a crucial driving force for future economy growth, where unmanned aerial vehicles serve as key devices for transportation and logistics [1,2].
To meet the long-range operation requirements, the energy density of rechargeable batteries is expected to exceed 600 Wh kg−1 [3].
The current commercial lithium-ion batteries can hardly achieve an actual energy density beyond 400 Wh kg−1 due to the limitations of the lithium ion interca­ lation reaction mechanism [4–7].
To this end, developing advanced rechargeable batteries with practical high energy density is highly required to meet these requirements [8,9].

Lithium‒sulfur (Li‒S) batteries afford an ultra-high theoretical en­ ergy density of 2600 Wh kg−1, making them one of the most promising candidates as next-generation high-energy-density recharge battery systems [10–13].
Typical Li‒S batteries rely on solid‒liquid‒solid conversion between elemental sulfur, dissolved lithium polysulfides (LiPSs), and solid lithium sulfide (Li2S) in ether-based electrolyte [14–16].

The soluble LiPSs avoid direct conversion between the elec­ tronic and ionic insulated sulfur and Li2S and facilitate their deposition and dissolution by chemical disproportionation and comproportionation reactions, thereby contributing to high utilization of the cathode active materials and high energy density of Li‒S batteries [17–19].
However, the dissolved LiPSs chemically react with lithium metal and inevitably corrode the lithium anode continuously, which is widely acknowledged to cause the shuttle effect [20–22].

The corrosion of lithium anode by the dissolved LiPSs irreversibly consumes the limited active lithium reservoir [23], and more importantly, generates low-valence sulfur species on surface of lithium anode to induce uneven lithium deposition and massive generation of inactive lithium [24–26].
The severe corro­ sion of lithium anode by the dissolved LiPSs results in rapid failure of Li‒ S batteries and restricts their practical application.
The dissolved LiPSs are solvated in electrolyte.
The solvation struc­ ture of LiPSs greatly influences the reaction kinetics of LiPSs and the Li–S battery performances [27–30].

Li–S battery cycling stability [31–33].
Typically, weakly-solvating electrolyte is constructed by introducing low donor number (DN) co-solvents.
For instance, Kaskel and co-workers constructed a weakly-solvating electrolyte by using a 1,1,2,2-tetrafluorethyl-2,2,3, 3-tetrafluorpropyl ether co-solvent [34].
The cycling lifespan of Li‒S pouch cells was prolonged by three times accordingly.

Hou et al. further studied the solvation structure of LiPSs in weakly-solvating electrolyte by partially replacing conventional high-DN 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) and 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) solvents with a low-DN di-isopropyl sulfide (DIPS) co-solvent [35].
A LiPS encapsulating solvation structure was identified via molecular dynamics simulation, mainly constructed by a DME-dominated inner solvation shell and a DIPS-dominated outer solvation shell.
A longer cycling lifespan of 100 cycles was achieved in Li‒S pouch cells with the help of this weakly-solvating electrolyte.
Up to the present, weakly-solvating Li–S batteries have demonstrated promi­ nent advantages in realizing long cycling lifespan under practical working conditions.

Generally, the weakly-solvating electrolytes protect the lithium anode without harming the sulfur redox kinetics under flooded elec­ trolyte conditions as the LiPSs are fully solvated to guarantee smooth sulfur redox kinetics [36,37].
However, massive electrolyte usage inevitably reduces the actual energy density of Li‒S batteries [38].
The electrolyte usage is usually described by the ratio of electrolyte volume to sulfur mass (E/S ratio) [39].
Li‒S batteries can hardly achieve an energy density over 400 Wh kg−1 when the E/S ratio is higher than 5 μL mg−1 [40].
Obviously, lean-electrolyte conditions are the prerequisite to achieve practical high-energy-density Li‒S batteries.

Nevertheless, lean-electrolyte Li–S batteries suffer from highly sluggish sulfur redox kinetics due to high LiPS concentration or even LiPS saturation, and the actual performances are greatly degraded regarding the discharge ca­ pacity, cell polarization, and rate responses [41–44].

The above chal­ lenges are even more severe in weakly-solvating Li‒S batteries due to the lower solvating power of the electrolyte with low-DN co-solvents [45], leading to unexpected rapid cell failure due to the dramatic degradation of the sulfur redox kinetics [46–48].

To develop Li‒S bat­ teries with both high energy density and long cycling lifespan, in-depth kinetics evaluation and targeted kinetic promotion strategies are essential for the weakly-solvating Li‒S batteries under lean-electrolyte conditions.
Herein, the sulfur redox kinetics under lean-electrolyte conditions is systematically evaluated in weakly-solvating Li‒S batteries to guide targeted kinetic promotion strategy design.
Typical weakly-solvating electrolyte is constructed by using DIPS as the low-DN co-solvent.

Tak­ ing kinetic polarization as the key indicator, a galvanostatic intermittent titration technique combined electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (GITT‒EIS) method is employed to decouple the total polarization into activation, concentration, and ohmic polarizations under different E/S ratios.

By excluding the minimal anode polarization, the cathode acti­ vation polarization at the Li2S nucleation stage increases by 640 % as the electrolyte usage decreases and occupies 61 % of the total polarization under lean-electrolyte conditions.

Furthermore, the activation energy of the interfacial charge transfer process of Li2S nucleation increases by 29 % at higher LiPS concentration, together identifying the cathode inter­ facial charge transfer kinetics at the Li2S nucleation stage as the main limiting factor.

Due to the reduced surface reaction rate at higher sulfur concentration, the Li2S nucleation changes from a three-dimensional diffusion-controlled hemisphere morphology to a two-dimensional sur­ face reaction-controlled needle morphology.

Accordingly, the size of the Li2S nuclei decreases from 184 to 63 nm and the thickness of the Li2S deposition layer decreases from 262 to 187 nm as the sulfur concen­ tration increases, in correspondence to the degraded deposition capacity by 41 %.

To accelerate the lean-electrolyte sulfur redox kinetics in weakly-solvating Li‒S batteries, a lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imidebased electrolyte (LiFSI electrolyte) is designed to achieve a high discharge capacity of 984 mAh g−1 and 50 stable cycles at a high rate of 0.2 C under a low E/S ratio of 5 μL mg−1.
Furthermore, an actual energy density of 410 Wh kg−1 is achieved in 5 Ah Li‒S pouch cells with the LiFSI electrolyte.

This work identifies the surface reaction-controlled Li2S deposition kinetics as the main kinetic challenge and highlights the LiPS solvation structure regulation strategy to accelerate the sulfur redox kinetics in lean-electrolyte weakly-solvating Li–S batteries. 2.

Results and discussion The weakly-solvating electrolyte was constructed by using DIPS as the low-DN co-solvent, and the thermodynamics and kinetics of Li‒S batteries using the weakly-solvating electrolyte were systematically analyzed under lean-electrolyte conditions.
Li‒S coin cells with the cathode sulfur loading of 4.0 mgS cm−2 and gradually decreased E/S ratios of 12, 8, 6, 5, or 4.5 μL mg−1 were assembled.
GITT at a current density of 0.1 C (1 C = 1672 mA g−1) was conducted on the coin cells to decouple the thermodynamics and kinetics (Figure S1‒S5).

Concretely, the thermodynamic voltage curves were obtained via connecting the final voltage points of each relaxation stage along the degree of discharge or charge and the connection of the final voltage points of each galvanostatic discharge or charge stage constituted the kinetic voltage curves (Fig. 1a).

For the discharge process, the thermodynamic voltage of the first discharge plateau slightly decreases as the electrolyte volume decreases, which is resulted from increased LiPS concentration in electrolyte [49].
Besides, the thermodynamic voltage of the second discharge plateau is basically overlapped at 2.173 V under different E/S ratio conditions.
Meantime, the variation of the thermodynamic voltage during the charge processes is basically the reverse of the discharge process under different E/S ratios.
Therefore, the lean-electrolyte con­ ditions have little effect on the thermodynamics of weakly-solvating Li‒ S batteries.
The kinetic polarization under different E/S ratios was further analyzed by calculating the difference between the thermodynamic voltage and the kinetic voltage.

When the E/S ratio decreases from 12 to 6 μL mg−1, the discharge polarizations are basically not changed at around 100 mV at the Li2S nucleation stage (Figure S6), suggesting the electrolyte amount is enough for smooth cathode reactions within this flooded E/S ratio range.

However, when the E/S ratio decreases from 6 to 4.5 μL mg−1, the discharge kinetic polarization rapidly increases from 96 to 300 mV at the Li2S nucleation stage and the kinetic voltage reaches as low as 1.868 V.

Comparingly, the kinetic voltage curves during the charge process are basically overlapped under different E/S ratios, indicating the kinetics of the charge process is barely affected by the electrolyte amount variation (Figure S7).
Therefore, the sluggish ki­ netics of the discharge process, especially at the Li2S nucleation stage, is the main problem of weakly-solvating Li‒S batteries under leanelectrolyte conditions.
The kinetics of the sulfur cathode and the lithium anode together contribute to the total kinetic polarization of Li‒S batteries.
The kinetic polarization of lithium anode under lean-electrolyte conditions was further estimated to quantify the portion of anode polarization within the total kinetic polarization.
Li | Li symmetric cells with 0, 1, or 4 M[S] LiPS electrolyte were assembled and cycled at a current density of 0.72 mA cm−2 equaling to the current density of the Li‒S coin cells at 0.1 C (Fig. 1b).

The bulk resistances of the Li | Li symmetric cells were determined by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) mea­ surements and the anode kinetic polarization under different sulfur concentrations was compared after eliminating the ohmic polarization (Figure S8‒S10, see more details in Supplementary Information).
The anode kinetic polarizations under sulfur concentrations of 0, 1, and 4 M[S] are all smaller than 16 mV, which only occupies 5 % of the total kinetic polarization maximally (Fig. 1c).
Therefore, the high kinetic polarization of weakly-solvating Li‒S batteries under lean-electrolyte conditions is resulted from the sluggish cathode kinetics.
To reveal the key kinetic limiting factor of the sulfur cathode in leanelectrolyte weakly-solvating Li‒S batteries, the cathode kinetic polari­ zation was further decoupled.

quantitatively decouple the total polarization into activation (ηac), concentration (ηcon), and ohmic polarization (ηohm) according to their dependence on the relaxation time (Figure S11‒S15, see more details in Supplementary Information) [50].
The ηac rapidly increases to the peak value at the Li2S nucleation stage during discharge, and then decreases by the end of discharge (Figure S16).
The ηcon gradually increases at the beginning of discharge and becomes stable after Li2S nucleation (Figure S17).
When the discharge process reaches 90 % DOD, the ηcon rapidly increases to above 300 mV and causes the termination of discharge.
Besides, the ηohm also reaches its peak value at the Li2S nucleation stage and then decreases eventually (Figure S18).
Obviously, the Li2S nucleation stage is the most kinetically sluggish stage as all the three kinetic polarizations reach a high value at this stage (Fig. 2a).
Once the Li2S nucleation stage is passed, the polarizations of Li‒S batteries gradually decrease.
The three polarizations at the Li2S nucleation stage are quantitatively compared under different E/S ratios to locate the key kinetic limiting factor.
The ηac is 25 mV at the Li2S nucleation stage at the E/S ratio of 12 μL mg−1, and the ηcon and ηohm are 60 and 7 mV under this electrolyte condition, respectively (Fig. 2b).
The ηac reaches 44 mV when the E/S ratio decreases to 6 μL mg−1.
The low ηac indicates the cathode con­ version kinetics is smooth under flooded electrolyte conditions.
How­ ever, the ηac rapidly increases to 185 mV when the E/S ratio further decreases to 4.5 μL mg−1, while the ηcon and ηohm are only 78 and 38 mV, respectively.
Furthermore, the polarization ratios of ηac to ηcon (ηac/ηcon) and ηac to ηohm (ηac/ηohm) at different E/S ratios are calculated to demonstrate the rapid increase of ηac over ηcon and ηohm.
The ηac/ηcon is 0.7 at the E/S ratio of 6 μL mg−1 and reaches 2.4 when the E/S ratio further decreases to 4.5 μL mg−1.
Similarly, the ηac/ηohm is 2.2 at the E/S ratio of 6 μL mg−1 and reaches 4.9 at the E/S ratio of 4.5 μL mg−1.
Obviously, the ηac is the key kinetic limiting factor of weakly-solvating Li‒S batteries under lean-electrolyte working conditions.

The kinetic polarization at the sulfur dissolution (10 % DOD) and the Li2S deposition stages (70 % DOD) were also analyzed.

At the sulfur dissolution stage, the ηac increases from 17 to 53 mV when the E/S ratio decreases from 6 to 4.5 μL mg−1 and is 13 and 33 mV higher than the ηcon and ηohm at the E/S ratio of 4.5 μL mg−1, respectively (Figure S19).
The ηac is also the dominant kinetic polarization component.

At the Li2S growth stage, the three polarizations are generally stable at different E/S ratios (Figure S20), indicating the overall kinetics at the Li2S growth stage is not violently affected by the electrolyte amount.

To further confirm the sluggish kinetics of the cathode interfacial charge transfer process under lean-electrolyte working conditions, the activation energy at the Li2S nucleation stage under different sulfur concentrations was measured according to the Arrhenius relationship.
Three-electrode Li | Li2S8 cells were assembled with 2, 4, or 6 M[S] Li2S8 electrolyte, where a lithium coated copper wire served as the reference electrode.
The sulfur mass in the Li | Li2S8 cells with different sulfur concentration electrolytes was the same by controlling the electrolyte addition amount.
The Li | Li2S8 cells were discharged to the Li2S nucleation stage and the EIS spectra of the cells in a wide temperature range were recorded.
Distribution of relaxation time (DRT) analysis was then conducted to decouple the interfacial charge transfer process from the overall cathodic electrochemical processes (Figure S21‒S23) [51–53].
The cathode interfacial charge transfer activation energy was obtained through the Arrhenius plots (Fig. 2c).
The activation energy reaches 193 kJ mol−1 in 6 M[S] Li2S8 electrolyte, which is 43 kJ mol−1 higher than that in 2 M[S] Li2S8 electrolyte.

The increased activation energy as the sulfur concentration increases demonstrates an exponen­ tial decline of the reaction rate coefficient under lean-electrolyte con­ ditions according to the Arrhenius equation.

In summary, ηac is the dominant kinetic polarization, and the interfacial charge transfer ki­ netics is confirmed as the critical limiting factor of weakly-solvating Li‒ S batteries under lean-electrolyte conditions.

To further correlate the lean-electrolyte sulfur redox kinetics with the cathode active material utilization, the Li2S nucleation and deposi­ tion behaviors at different sulfur concentrations were observed.
Li | Li2S8 cells with the sulfur concentration of 2, 4, or 6 M[S] Li2S8 were disassembled at the Li2S nucleation stage.
The Li2S nucleation mor­ phologies were observed via scanning electron microscope (SEM, Fig. 3a).
The deposited Li2S is hemispherical at the sulfur concentration of 2 M[S], while the morphology changes to needle-like when the sulfur concentration increases to 4 and 6 M[S].
The nucleus size of Li2S was further quantitatively analyzed (Figure S24‒S26).
The average Li2S nucleus size in 6 M[S] Li2S8 electrolyte is 63 nm and is 66 % smaller than that in 2 M[S] Li2S8 electrolyte (Fig. 3b).

The lower Li2S nucleation re­ action rate results in the Li2S nucleus changes from a diffusioncontrolled three-dimensional hemisphere-like morphology to a surface reaction-controlled two-dimensional needle-like morphology.

Controlled by the surface reaction, only a little amount of LiPS is able to be electrochemically reduced and form Li2S nuclei with smaller size on the conductive surface, which results in larger kinetic polarization to stabilize the small Li2S nuclei.
The Li2S deposition morphologies at the end of discharge were further studied.
The Li2S deposition keeps the hemisphere-like morphology in 2 M[S] Li2S8 electrolyte (Figure S27).
Surprisingly, a hemisphere-like morphology composited by the needle-like Li2S is eventually formed in 4 M[S] Li2S8 electrolyte (Figure S28).
When the sulfur concentration increases to 6 M[S], the needle-like Li2S constitutes the bulk with irregular shape (Figure S29).
The deposition amount of Li2S is evaluated by comparing the Li2S deposition thickness (Figure S30).

The deposition thickness of Li2S at the sulfur concentration of 2 M[S] is 262 nm and decreases to 226 and 187 nm at the sulfur concentration of 4 and 6 M[S], respectively (Fig. 3c and Figure S31‒ S32).
The thinner Li2S deposition layer at higher sulfur concentration is resulted from higher degree of surface reaction-controlled Li2S deposi­ tion and corresponding two-dimensional Li2S deposition.
Thinner deposition thickness brings more rapid conductive surface coverage by the insulating Li2S deposits, thereby blocking the subsequent reactions.
To validate the above argument, Li | Li2S8 cells with the same sulfur mass but different sulfur concentration of 2, 4, or 6 M[S] were poten­ tiostatically discharged at 2.10 V (Figure S33‒S35).
The deposition capacity is 124 mAh g−1 when the sulfur concentration is 2 M[S], and decreases to 97 and 73 mAh g−1 at the sulfur concentration of 4 and 6 Fig. 3.

Therefore, the surface reaction controlled Li2S nucleation and growth under lean-electrolyte working conditions leads to rapid conductive surface coverage, premature termination of Li2S deposition, enlarged concentration polarization, and consequent discharge capacity degradation in weakly-solvating Li–S batteries (Fig. 3e).
Li salt anions are able to coordinate with LiPSs and are expected to accelerate the sulfur redox kinetics in weakly-solvating electrolyte under lean-electrolyte conditions [54–56].
A LiFSI electrolyte was pre­ pared and applied in weakly-solvating Li‒S batteries under lean-electrolyte working conditions.

The rate performances of Li‒S batteries with the LiFSI electrolyte or the conventional lithium bis (trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide-based electrolyte (LiTFSI electrolyte) were firstly evaluated in Li‒S coin cells with the cathode sulfur loading of 4.0 mgS cm−2 and an E/S ratio of 4.5 μL mg−1.
The Li‒S cells with the LiFSI electrolyte cycle stably at 0.3 C (1 C = 1672 mA g−1) and deliver a high discharge capacity of 798 mAh g−1 (Fig. 4a, S36, and S37).
Com­ paringly, the Li‒S cells with the LiTFSI electrolyte can only work at 0.1 C so that the maximum cyclable current density is improved by twice.
Besides, the Li‒S cells deliver a high discharge capacity of 980 mAh g−1 at the current density of 0.1 C in the LiFSI electrolyte, which is 180 mAh g−1 higher than that in the LiTFSI electrolyte.
The medium voltage of the Li‒S cells was further analyzed to demonstrate the kinetic advantages of the LiFSI electrolyte (Figure S38).

At high current densities of 0.2 and 0.3 C, the medium voltages in the LiFSI electrolyte are 1.90 and 1.82 V, while the Li‒S cells fail to overcome the huge polarization at the Li2S nucleation stage in the LiTFSI electrolyte.
Therefore, the LiFSI electro­ lyte successfully accelerates the interfacial charge transfer kinetics of weakly-solvating Li–S batteries under lean-electrolyte conditions.
Furthermore, the long-cycling capability of the LiFSI electrolyte was evaluated.
Li‒S coin cells with the LiFSI electrolyte at the E/S ratio of 5.0 μL mg−1 were assembled and cycled at the current density of 0.2 C (Figure S39).
The LiTFSI electrolyte can hardly guarantee smooth sulfur redox kinetics at high current density, and the Li‒S cells with the LiTFSI electrolyte fail immediately at 0.2 C.

Comparingly, the Li‒S cells with the LiFSI electrolyte achieve a high discharge capacity of 984 mAh g−1 at 0.2 C and cycle stably for 50 times before the capacity reaches 60 % of the initial capacity.
The battery performances were further conducted using high sulfur loading cathodes of 7.0 mgS cm−2.
A maximum cycling rate of 0.25 C is achieved in the LiFSI electrolyte while the LiTFSI electrolyte only supports a maximum cycling rate of 0.15 C.

When the cycling rate changes back to 0.1 C, 15 stable cycles are achieved with the help of the LiFSI electrolyte, while the weakly-solvating Li‒S cells with the LiTFSI electrolyte fail rapidly after only one cycle at 0.1 C (Fig. 4b).
To demonstrate the kinetic promotion advantage of LiFSI, perfor­ mances of Li‒S pouch cell with the LiFSI electrolyte were further eval­ uated.
Rate performances were first evaluated in 3 Ah Li‒S pouch cells (Figure S40).
The Li‒S pouch cell with the LiFSI electrolyte delivers high discharge capacities of 1219, 1139, 1099, 1080, and 939 mAh g−1 at 0.025, 0.05, 0.08, 0.1, and 0.15 C, respectively (Fig. 4c).

In comparison, the Li‒S pouch cell with the LiTFSI electrolyte fails rapidly at 0.05 C and the discharge capacity is less than 200 mAh g−1 at higher rates due to the sluggish kinetics (Figure S41). 5 Ah Li‒S pouch cells with the LiFSI electrolyte were assembled and a high discharge capacity of 1150 mAh g−1 is delivered, which is 855 mAh g−1 higher than that in the LiTFSI electrolyte (Figure S42).
The actual energy density of the Li‒S pouch cell is 410 Wh kg−1 based on the total mass (Table S1 and S2).

Furthermore, an 8 Ah Li‒S pouch cell with the LiFSI electrolyte was assembled and a high discharge capacity of 1260 mAh g−1 is achieved at the 1st cycle, contributing to an actual energy density of 474 Wh kg−1 (Fig. 4d).
The high-energy-density pouch cell maintains 20 cycles and delivers an actual energy density of 412 Wh kg−1, during which the Coulombic ef­ ficiency is stable around 99 % (Fig. 4e and S43).
The performance stands out as one of the best pouch cells among the recent reports (Fig. 4f and Table S3).

Therefore, Li‒S batteries with both high energy density and long cycling lifespan can be achieved by the LiFSI electrolyte that effectively accelerates the sulfur redox kinetics in weakly-solvating Li–S batteries under lean-electrolyte conditions. 3.
Conclusion In conclusion, systematic cathode kinetic analysis is conducted on weakly-solvating Li‒S batteries under lean-electrolyte conditions.
The sluggish interfacial charge transfer kinetics is identified as the key ki­ netic limiting factor by quantitative polarization decoupling and acti­ vation energy measurements.

The Li2S deposition process changes from diffusion-controlled to surface reaction-controlled as the sulfur con­ centration increases, leading to smaller Li2S nucleation size and thinner Li2S deposition thickness corresponding to rapid coverage of the conductive surface and consequent low deposition capacity.
A LiFSI electrolyte is proposed to accelerate the interfacial charge transfer ki­ netics, and weakly-solvating Li‒S batteries achieve a high discharge Fig. 4.

capacity of 985 mAh g−1 at a low E/S ratio of 5.0 μL mg−1 and high current density of 0.2 C as well as 50 stable cycles.
Furthermore, a 410 Wh kg−1 Li‒S pouch cell is realized in the LiFSI electrolyte.

This work reveals the surface reaction-controlled Li2S deposition kinetics as the origin of discharge capacity degradation of weakly-solvating Li‒S bat­ teries under lean-electrolyte working conditions.
Solvation structure regulation is demonstrated to effectively accelerate the Li2S deposition kinetics and achieve Li‒S battery performance promotion.

Experimental section 1.1.

Raw materials All the raw materials including sulfur (S), lithium sulfide (Li2S), lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI), lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI), multi-walled carbon nanotubes (CNTs), poly(vinylidenefluoride) (PVDF), Nmethylpyrrolidone (NMP), lithium nitrate (LiNO3), 1,3-dioxolane (DOL), 1,2- dimethoxyethane (DME), di-isopropyl sulfide (DIPS), carbon papers, aluminum (Al) foils, copper (Cu) foils, polypropylene (PP) membranes (Celgard 2500), lithium (Li) metal foils, 2025 coin cell shells, and 2032 coin cell shells were purchased from commercial sources and directly used without further purification. 1.2.
Evaluation of thermodynamics and kinetics under different E/S ratios 1.2.1.
Sulfur cathode preparation Sulfur and CNT were first mixed in a batch with a mass ratio of 7:3.
The mixture was then ball-milled with PVDF binder at a weight ratio of 9:1 in NMP to form a slurry.
The obtained slurry was then coated on Al foils and fully dried at 60°C for 24 h.
The sulfur cathode was cut into small disks with a diameter of 13.0 mm.
The sulfur content was 63 wt.% and the areal sulfur loading was 4.0 or 7.0 mgS cm−2. 1.2.2.
Weakly-solvating electrolyte preparation The weakly-solvating electrolyte was mixed solvents of DME/DOL/DIPS (1:0.75:0.25, molar ratio) with 1.0 mol L−1 LiTFSI and 5.0 wt.% LiNO3.

To prepare the Li2S8 electrolyte with a sulfur concentration of 1, 2, 4, or 6 M[S], 0.625, 1.25, 2.5, or 3.75 mmol Li2S and 4.375, 8.75, 17.5, or 26.25 mmol S were mixed in 5 mL weaklysolvating electrolyte at a molar ratio of 1:7 respectively, and then stirred at 60°C.
SI2 the above procedures were conducted in an Ar-filled glove box with water and oxygen contents below 0.1 ppm. 1.2.3.

Weakly-solvating Li‒S cell assembly and electrochemical measurement Weakly-solvating Li–S cells under a series of different E/S ratios were assembled and used for galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) tests.

Concretely, the sulfur cathodes with a diameter of 13.0 mm were used as the cathode, lithium metal foils with a diameter of 15.0 mm and a thickness of 50 μm were adopted as the anode, PP membranes with a diameter of 19.0 mm were used as the separator, and the electrolyte was the weakly-solvating electrolyte.
The E/S ratio was 12, 8, 6, 5, or 4.5 μL mg−1.
All the components were sealed with standard 2032 coin cell shells and all the above procedures were conducted in an argon-filled glove box with water and oxygen contents below 0.1 ppm.
GITT tests were performed using the weakly-solvating Li–S cells to locate the thermodynamic and kinetic voltages.
The GITT curves were obtained by a series of galvanostatic discharge or charge processes of 6.0 min at 0.1 C (1 C = 1672 mA g−1) followed by 60.0 min rest at each step.
All the electrochemical tests were performed on a Neware multichannel battery cycler. 1.3.
Polarization decoupling 1.3.1.
Evaluation of the influence of lithium anode Li | Li symmetric cells were assembled and used to evaluate the polarization of the lithium anode.

Concretely, two pieces of lithium metal foil with a diameter of 15.0 mm and thickness of 50 μm were used as the electrodes, and PP membranes with a diameter of 19.0 mm were used as the separator. 40 μL of 1 or 4 M[S] Li2S8 electrolyte was added
SI3 to the symmetric cells, respectively.
All the components were sealed with standard 2025 coin-type cells.
The Li | Li symmetric cells were galvanostatically cycled at 0.72 mA cm−2 and 3.60 mAh cm−2 which corresponded to the full-cell conditions.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was carried out on a Solartron 1470E electrochemical workstation.
EIS was performed using the potentiostatic mode at the open circuit voltage.
A sinusoidal voltage with an amplitude of 10 mV and a frequency range from 0.1 Hz to 10 kHz was applied.
The intercept at the Z’ axis was regarded as the ohmic resistance.
The voltage at the 3rd cycle of the Li | Li symmetric cells was regarded as the total polarization, while the ohmic polarization was obtained through the ohmic resistance multiplying the current.
The kinetic polarization of the anode was obtained through the total polarization minus the ohmic polarization. 1.3.2.
Decoupling of activation, concentration, and ohmic polarization.

A GITT‒EIS method was developed to decouple the total polarization (ηtotal) into activation (ηac), concentration (ηcon), and ohmic polarizations (ηohm) in weakly-solvating Li–S batteries under a series of E/S ratios.
The weakly-solvating Li–S cells were assembled following the same procedure as in section 1.2.3.
The parameters of GITT were also the same as above involving a series of galvanostatic discharge processes of 6.0 min at a current density of 0.1 C followed by 60.0 min rest at each step.
An additional EIS measurement was conducted before each galvanostatic step to obtain the ohmic resistance (Rohm).
The EIS measurements were conducted in a frequency range from 0.1 Hz to 10 kHz.
The ohmic resistance was obtained from the intercept at the Z’ axis.
The ηtotal was determined as the voltage difference between the thermodynamic voltage and the kinetic voltage of the weakly-solvating Li–S batteries.

SI4 recovery during the rest step in GITT was resulted from the concentration gradient built in the discharge step and was adopted as the ηcon. ηohm was determined by multiplying the ohmic resistance obtained through the EIS measurements with the applied current density. ηac was obtained though ηac = ηtotal ‒ ηohm ‒ ηcon.

The three kinetic polarizations of the sulfur cathode during the discharge process under different E/S ratios were further evaluated at three stages regarding sulfur dissolution, Li2S nucleation, and Li2S growth, respectively. 1.4.
Measurements of interfacial charge transfer activation energy Three-electrode Li | Li2S8 cells were assembled using 2, 4, or 6 M[S] Li2S8 electrolyte.
Commercial carbon papers were used as the working electrode and lithium metal foils with a diameter of 16.0 mm and thickness of 600 μm were adopted as the counter electrode.

Two pieces of PP membranes with a diameter of 19.0 mm were used as the separator and a Cu@Li reference electrode was placed between the two separators to avoid the contact with the other two electrodes. 70 μL of 2, 4, or 6 M[S] Li2S8 electrolyte was added to the Li | Li2S8 cells to guarantee sufficient electrolyte infiltration.
The three-electrode Li | Li2S8 cells were discharged to the Li2S nucleation stage which is at the beginning of the second voltage plateau at the current of 0.5 mA.
EIS measurements under 303, 308, 313, 318, or 323 K were carried out on the Solartron 1470E electrochemical workstation.

Distribution of relaxation time (DRT) analysis was conducted by applying the MATLAB GUI based DRT tools which are developed by Ciucci’s groups.[1] The parameters for DRT were based on the Gaussian discretization method with a regularization parameter of 10−4 and FWHM control of 0.5, where the inductive data was neglected during fitting.

Evaluation of Li2S nucleation and deposition behaviors 1.5.1 Morphology evaluation of Li2S nucleation and deposition Li | Li2S8 cells with a sulfur concentration of 2, 4, or 6 M[S] Li2S8 electrolyte were assembled.
Commercial carbon papers were used as the cathodic current collector and lithium metal foils with a diameter of 16.0 mm and thickness of 600 μm were adopted as the anode.

PP membranes with a diameter of 19.0 mm were used as the separator. 75 μL 2 M[S], 37.5 μL 4 M[S], or 25 μL 6 M[S] Li2S8 electrolyte were added into the Li | Li2S8 cells to control the active materials to be the same.
The Li | Li2S8 cells were discharged to the Li2S nucleation stage or the end of the Li2S deposition stage, respectively.
The discharged Li | Li2S8 cells were disassembled and the carbon papers were taken out and washed with pure DME until the color of the DME was not changed.
The morphology of Li2S was observed on a scanning electron microscope (SEM, FEI-Apreo C, FEI Ltd., USA) operated at 5.0 kV.

The Li2S nucleation size and deposition thickness were quantitatively measured by the Digital Micrograph software via the difference of the graph intensities. 1.5.2 Evaluation of Li2S deposition capacity Potentiostatic intermittent titration technique (PITT) was performed using the Li | Li2S8 cells to locate the voltage of Li2S deposition.
The cells were potentiostatically discharged at 2.30, 2.25, 2.20, and 2.15 V for 10.0 h and then potentiostatically discharged at 2.10 and 2.05 V for 50.0 h.
The Li2S deposition occurs at 2.10 V and the corresponding deposition capacity was obtained by integration and compared under different sulfur concentrations.

Performance of lean-electrolyte Li‒S batteries using the LiFSI electrolyte The LiFSI electrolyte was prepared using mixed solvents of DME/DOL/DIPS (1:0.75:0.25, molar ratio) with 0.8 mol L−1 LiFSI, 0.2 mol L−1 LiTFSI, and 5.0 wt.% LiNO3.

The LiTFSI electrolyte was prepared using mixed solvents of DME/DOL/DIPS (1:0.75:0.25, molar ratio) with 1.0 mol L−1 LiTFSI and 5.0 wt.% LiNO3. 4.0 mgS cm−2 Li‒S cells with the LiFSI electrolyte or the LiTFSI electrolyte were assembled at the E/S ratio of 4.5 μL mg−1 and the rest configurations were kept the same with the above weakly-solvating electrolyte Li‒S cells.
To evaluate the rate performances, the Li‒S cells were activated at 0.05 C for two cycles and then cycled at 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.2, and 0.1 C for 3 cycles in order.
The Li‒S cells were cycled between 1.70–2.60 V on the Neware multichannel battery cycler.
To evaluate the long cycling performance, 4.0 mgS cm−2 Li‒S cells at the E/S ratio of 5 μL mg−1 were assembled.
The LiFSI electrolyte or the LiTFSI electrolyte was used as the electrolyte, respectively.
The Li‒S cells were activated at 0.05 and 0.1 C for two cycles and then galvanostatically cycled at 0.2 C between 1.70–2.60 V on the Neware multichannel battery cycler.
The lean-electrolyte kinetics under practical high sulfur loading conditions was further evaluated by assembling Li‒S cells with the sulfur loading of 7.0 mgS cm−2.
The LiFSI electrolyte or the LiTFSI electrolyte was used as the electrolyte, respectively.
The E/S ratio was 5 μL mg−1.
The 7.0 mgS cm−2 Li‒S cells were activated at 0.05 C for two cycles and then galvanostatically cycled at 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, and 0.25 C for 3 cycles.
The 7.0 mgS cm−2 Li‒S cells were then cycled at 0.1 C after the rate test.
The 7.0 mgS cm−2 Li‒S cells were cycled between 1.70–2.60 V on the Neware multichannel battery cycler.
Li–S pouch cell assembly and evaluation Sulfur cathodes were cut into 4.0 cm × 7.0 cm with a sulfur loading of 7.5–7.9 mgS cm−2 on a single side.
Lithium anodes were fabricated by rolling lithium metal foils on both sides of Cu foils and then cut into electrodes of the same size as the sulfur cathodes.
The thickness of the lithium foil was 75 μm on a single side.
The separator used in pouch cells was PP membranes or PE membranes.
The pouch cell electrolyte was the LiFSI electrolyte or the LiTFSI electrolyte.
To prove the kinetic promotion effect of LiFSI, Li‒S pouch cells were assembled for performances evaluation.
Five sulfur cathodes (7.8 mgS cm−2 on a single side) and six lithium anodes were stacked layer-by-layer and separated by PP membranes.
All the electrodes were set in parallel connection and then put in a package.
Then, the LiFSI electrolyte or the LiTFSI electrolyte was injected into the pouch cells and the E/S ratio was 2.8 gele gS−1.
After that, the 3 Ah Li‒S pouch cells were vacuumed (‒65 kPa) and sealed for further electrochemical tests.
The 3 Ah Li‒S pouch cells were discharged at 0.025 C at the 1st cycle for activation after resting for 12.0 h.
Then the Li‒S pouch cells were discharged at 0.05, 0.08, 0.1, and 0.15 C for two cycles and the charge current density was kept at 0.025 C (1 C = 1000 mA g−1).
Furthermore, 5 Ah Li‒S pouch cells were assembled with nine sulfur cathodes (7.9 mgS cm−2 on a single side) and ten lithium anodes using PE separators and the E/S ratio was 2.5 gele gS−1.
The 5 Ah pouch cells were discharged at 0.05 C after resting for 12.0 h.
The 8 Ah Li‒S pouch cell was assembled with fifteen sulfur cathodes (7.5 mgS cm−2 on a single side) and sixteen lithium anodes using PE separators and the E/S ratio was 2.8 gele gS−1.
The 8 Ah Li‒S pouch cell was cycled at 0.025 C after resting for 12.0 h.
